A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CyberGym and retain matching benchmark content. Their main texts, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 Section 3 and Appendix D report original agent evaluations, behavioral analyses, and vulnerability-discovery results, including 15 zero-days.

after.justification: v2 Sections 4–5 and Appendices D–F report original evaluations, incomplete-patch investigations, case studies, and 35 zero-day discoveries.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, four input levels, and PoC generation loop remain intact. v2 Section 5 adds a dedicated incomplete-patch identification procedure using fuzzy matching of sanitizer reports followed by manual root-cause confirmation. The few-shot filtering emphasized in v2 was already documented in v1 Appendix C.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 1,507-instance benchmark, matching lists of 188 projects and 28 crash types, four task levels, and discovery evaluation covering 431 projects with 1,748 executables. v1's isolated reference to 187 projects becomes 188; the matching project tables establish no corresponding coverage addition.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-5 and Claude-Sonnet-4 to the nine-model OpenHands comparison and thinking comparisons. GPT-5 also joins GPT-4.1 in open-ended discovery. The four agent frameworks remain unchanged; these are additions within the existing comparison families.

E3.justification: v1 Section 2.1 defines both reproduction and post-patch vulnerability detection as successful outcomes; v2 Section 3.2 narrows benchmark success to reproduction and analyzes post-patch crashes separately. Added GPT-5 experiments compare minimal and high reasoning effort. Both versions retain a 300-task thinking comparison and the previously stated agent budgets and iteration limits.

E4.justification: v2 adds a systematic historical incomplete-patch audit, a GDAL patch case, and analysis of zero-day persistence duration. It extends thinking and PoC-length analyses to additional models, replaces the GPT-4.1 step-count analysis with Claude-Sonnet-4, and adds comparative failure cases in Appendix F. The command-usage analysis and two earlier appendix cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-trial counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its agent evaluations. v1's recommendation of 30 repeated fuzzing runs describes prior evaluation guidance, not this work's experimental practice.

E6.justification: The original nine-model reproduction scores are retained, while v2 adds Claude-Sonnet-4's 17.9% full-benchmark result and GPT-5's 7.7% versus 22.0% results in the 300-task reasoning comparison. Expanded discovery experiments report 35 zero-days versus 15, alongside 17 historical incomplete patches. v2 also changes the reported agent-union rate from 18.5% to 18.4% and removes per-method post-patch result series and model-union summaries.

T1.justification: Neither version contains formal theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations. v2's new preliminaries explain program versions, sanitizers, and fuzzing without introducing substantive mathematical content.

C1.justification: The central claims of a challenging, realistic benchmark and agents' ability to discover zero-days remain. v2 adds historical incomplete-patch detection as an explicit contribution and strengthens claims that CyberGym provides a difficulty ladder and a proxy for real-world cybersecurity capabilities.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that benchmark/discovery rankings support CyberGym's proxy value and that 100 steps balance solvability against resource use. It strengthens the reasoning against contamination effects, while dropping v1's explicit discussions of fuzzing-source bias and binary-only applicability. The principal complexity and agent-failure interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies checkpoints for the two added models, reports aggregate API expenditure and H100 hours, and specifies binary search for locating patch commits. Existing prompts, hardware details, agent commits, and code/data access information remain. However, v1's explicit provenance breakdown of 1,368 ARVO instances and 139 newly collected instances is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning through comparisons with AutoAdvExBench, BountyBench, and SEC-Bench and a new benchmark comparison table emphasizing scale and zero-day impact. It removes the PentestGPT comparison and the detailed discussion relating agents to traditional and LLM-guided fuzzing.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and substantial portions of the main narrative are rewritten. Related work moves earlier, a preliminaries subsection and dedicated security-impact section appear, ethics moves out of the appendix, and supplementary material is reorganized into Appendices D–F. These changes substantially alter the document's structure and emphasis.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview and experimental plots, including changing the model comparison to horizontal bars, adds a benchmark comparison table, and removes the pie charts and UpSet plot. Statistics move to Appendix B, case-trace displays expand and reflow, and the page template and visual styling change throughout.

improvement.justification: The added frontier-model comparisons, documented patch-validation procedure and GDAL example, and comparative failure cases improve empirical depth and interpretability beyond v1's existing evaluation. These gains are tempered by removal of per-method post-patch results and provenance detail, while the stronger real-world proxy claim rests on only two discovery models. The net improvement is useful but limited.
